1.	Has there been in effect in the Post Office Department a night differential in favour of employees obliged to be on duty between the hours of 5 p.m. and 7 a.m.? If so. what have been the terms of such a night differential?
2.	Has any such night differential been discontinued, or is it being discontinued, in connection with the institution of the five-day 40-hour week amongst post office employees? If so, for what reason?
3.	Have any protests been received against the abolition of said night differential, and is consideration being given to maintaining the said night differential?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
1.	Yes. Seven hours night duty has been accepted in lieu of eight hours.
2.	Yes. It is proposed to implement the five-day 40-hour week for all shifts.
3.	No formal representations have been received, but reports of a meeting in Vancouver indicate some confusion. Night differential as previously applied disappears with the adoption of the five-day 40-hour week, but the department recognizing the inconvenience of night work has recommended a cash allowance for night duty at points where the five-day 40-hour week goes into effect.
The cash allowance for the additional one and a half hours worked and the inconvenience will be approximately $6 per worker per week for full-time night duty.
Employees will also have the benefit of one more day free from duty each week. In other words their hours of duty will be confined to five days instead of six as at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps I could make an oral statement on these two questions. It is not in the public interest to answer these questions. The security panel acts anonymously. It does not pass orders but rather recommendations to the deputy head. In my opinion it is not in the public interest to say why people were dismissed from the service, whether it was on security grounds or otherwise. I hope my hon. friend will be satisfied to drop these two questions.

Mr. Speaker, I tried to frame these questions in such a way that the answers, if given, would be purely factual and the answers would not give a lead to the personnel of the panel or be of aid in tracing the name of a person. I would hope that the minister might reconsider the matter and, in view of the way in which the questions are phrased, might reconsider whether or not it is possible to give an answer.

The first question does not ask for the names of any people dealt with by the panel. It only requests the names of the panel and how often it meets. What is the procedure on appeal from a decision of a security officer or from the panel itself? Again it would seem to me that is the type of factual information that would not reveal any security material that it is proper not to disclose.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not wish to debate the subject. Whether answering the questions would disclose a security matter or not is a matter of opinion. I suppose if only one man has been dismissed from his department, and we say that one man was dismissed for security reasons, it is pretty obvious who the one man is. I see no good purpose to be served. As I understand the rule, the question can be asked and the government can decide whether it is to be answered or not. I think the decision of the government must be that these two questions cannot be answered.
That they will not be answered.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for 83276-167
Inquiries of the Ministry Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked me, upon what authority in connection with the commitment for contempt of court of Edward Bryan of Cornwall, Chief Justice McRuer could in fact substitute the sentence of a fine for imprisonment after sentence had been commenced. The question raised by the hon. member had to do with the administration of justice, which is a provincial responsibility. I had no material before me indicating the basis of the chief justice's authority to make such an order. I had no responsibility for having such material before me. I therefore declined at that time to answer my hon. friend's question.
While there may be a distinct difference of opinion as to the propriety of asking such a question in this house, once it has been asked I think it would be unfair to Chief Justice McRuer that I should not complete the record of this incident by placing upon it Chief Justice McRuer's own statement as to his authority to make this order which the hon. member for Prince Albert has questioned. I have accordingly secured from Chief Justice McRuer the following statement, which is in the third person:
The matter was brought before the court by an application made by Mr. Kelly, the counsel for the accused Balcombe in the case of Regina v. Balcombe, and the material upon which the order was based was placed before the chief justice McRuer on this application. The chief justice, exercising the inherent power vested in a judge of a court of superior jurisdiction, directed that the publishers and the distributor in the Cornwall area should be brought before the court to show cause why they should not be committed for contempt of court. In imposing the penalty, Chief Justice McRuer exercised the inherent power vested in a judge of any court of superior jurisdiction in a matter of this character, and likewise the chief justice in remitting part of Mr. Bryan's sentence, exercised an inherent power that is vested in a judge who imposes such a sentence when he considers that the service of part of the sentence may have sufficiently purged the contempt of the prisoner.
The statement of fact in the question-
That is, Mr. Speaker, the question which the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked me yesterday.
-that a fine was substituted for imprisonment, is not correct. The order releasing Mr. Bryan was made upon condition not that he should pay a fine, but that he should pay the costs of the application of Mr. Kelly, the counsel for the accused Balcombe.
Statements appearing in the press that this order was made after representations had been heard by the chief justice from citizens of Cornwall are likewise incorrect. The order was made entirely on Chief Justice McRuer's own initiative after consultation with the crown counsel in the Balcombe case.

At this stage I should like to make a brief statement to outline in a general way what is involved in this resolution. As the committee knows, the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which was first enacted in 1942, was designed to provide legislative authority for the carrying out of the various forms of training for discharged members of the armed forces, and for such forms of vocational training or assistance for vocational training as could be foreseen as coming within the immediate post-war period.
The act provides that all training may be undertaken by provincial authorities under [Mr. Garson.l

agreements between the provincial and federal governments providing for federal financial assistance.
There has been established under the act a vocational training advisory council which includes representatives of the provinces of employers, of organized labour, of women, of veterans and of other interested groups. The work of this council has been of very great assistance to the administration of the act. In passing I should like to pay tribute to the excellent work that has been done by the members of the council. Part of the amendments proposed here are for the special purpose, which I shall indicate later, of increasing the number from 16 to 20.
It is proposed to revise the wording of certain provisions of the act in the light of present-day training requirements. These differ in some respects from those existing at the time the act first came into force. These changes have been discussed with provincial authorities and the advisory council has expressed the desirability of the changes in the act and in the training program itself.
Training programs are conducted under the provisions of the Vocational Training Coordination Act through federal-provincial agreements, namely, the vocational training agreement, the vocational schools' assistance agreement, the apprenticeship agreement and the correspondence courses agreement.
Under the provisions of the vocational training agreement, the federal government co-operates with the provinces in the following types of programs: (a) the training of former members of Her Majesty's forces who are approved for such training by the Department of Veterans Affairs; (b) training for unemployed workers referred by the national employment service and for whom such training is required to fit them for suitable employment; (c) trades training for members of the armed forces and the provision of civilian instructors for schools operated by the armed forces; (d) training of skilled and semi-skilled workers for defence production; (e) training of foremen and supervisors in industrial establishments; (f) training for young people from rural communities who are not served by the existing provincial school systems; (g) financial aid to needy worthy university students and to nurses in training.
That covers the vocational training agreement, Mr. Chairman. Under the terms of the vocational schools' assistance agreement, financial aid is provided to the provinces for the construction, equipment and operation of technical, vocational and trade schools of

less than university grades. I am sure hon. members will realize that in view of the great number of veterans who have been trained in skills under this act, the greater part of that program has been completed. In other words, the provinces, with the assistance of the federal government, have established a pretty substantial set-up of well-equipped vocational schools across the country; but it is under that section that that has been done.
Under the provisions of the third one, the apprenticeship agreement, training is provided in full-time and part-time classes for apprentices registered with departments of labour under the provisions of provincial apprenticeship acts.
I now come to the fourth group. Under the provisions of the correspondence agreement, the federal government shares with the provincial governments in the cost of the preparation of vocational correspondence courses which are made available under the same terms and conditions to students in all parts of Canada.

Why not wait for the bill?
Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to the minister answering them, but I do think the questions should be answered when we have the bill before us so that our questions may be relevant. I listened to the minister but of course one cannot get the gist of everything he said with regard to the amendments. While these matters sound all right on paper they certainly do not work out in practice as the paper indicates they should. I have talked a lot over the years about vocational training.
The limiting factors in regard to vocational training in this country are still present. First, if you are going to have a vocational training system in this country you must have schools. That is a first requirement. We have not the schools. We are not going to get the schools under the present financial arrangements among the dominion, provincial and municipal governments. The provincial and federal governments can say, and they have said, that they will contribute their share of the cost, and then it is passed right back to the municipality.
Seventy-five per cent of the municipalities across this country are not in a position to take advantage of that government offer and the result is that we do not have schools. I do not care what regulations you may write, if a community has not the facilities for training they will be valueless. That is No. 1. Some thinking must be done by the provincial and federal governments if we are going to have vocational training, and that thinking must be on the matter of financing the establishment of schools.
I come now to my second point. While the vocational training system did assist a large number of veterans, there were thousands of good soldiers who came back to this country after making the maximum contribution in the war and who were never able to take advantage of the regulations because of academic limitations. I have placed on the record a good many times figures showing the number of soldiers who came out of the last war, who never had a job and who had not got to the eighth grade in school. They went into the service and served four or five years and when they came back to this country they were unable to take up vocational training or get into any kind of


school. They went back to the ranks of the unemployed as untrained men. There were thousands in that class. No matter what the regulations are, even though you get schools, this type of person will not be able to take advantage of any kind of vocational training.
The same situation exists in connection with recruiting for the air force, army and navy. We are using very attractive slogans, we are saying to these young men, "Come in and we will give you a trade; make the army your future". There are thousands of sensible, clean-cut boys who are ready to go into the service, but they cannot pass the academic tests. Some of them came to see me in this building, boys of 19 or 20 years of age. When I asked them what about the service or the vocational training system they hung their heads and in many cases admitted that they had not got beyond the sixth grade. They have more brains than most hon. members in this house, including myself, though they have never had a chance to develop them. That is how you get potential gangsters or bank robbers. If the minister or the department or the government are going to take a look at this vocational training problem, then the first two things they must have a look at are the provision of schools across this country and the necessary instruction to enable these young people to take advantage of their opportunities.
If these young men of 19 and 20 years of age, who come from families numbering perhaps 12 to 15 members, have to go out and work instead of going through high school, in order to support other members of the family, then they will be in no position to take advantage of this scheme. Let us try and provide in the curriculum of the schools the academic instruction necessary to enable those young boys to take a vocational training course in diesel engines, electronics, or something else.
If we do not do that we will be wasting thousands upon thousands of potentially good citizens across this country. We gave that type of person a very raw deal in the aftermath of the war. He was good enough to fight but he was not sufficiently trained academically even to take a vocational training course, and he was discriminated against. I have said that many times in this house, and I believe now is the time we should assist them. We have unemployment in this country now. It may continue, though we hope not; but there are thousands of young fellows across this country today and unless we provide them with a means of

Vocational Training Co-ordination Act
getting into a place where they can get some training you are going to have trouble with them, and plenty of trouble.
What is essential now is not a whole lot more regulations, but the provision of schools and the necessary instruction to enable the young people of this country to get into these schools.
I believe it will be necessary to take a look at the present set-up in the services, because at the present time we are keeping out of the services thousands of young people who would perhaps make it their career if they had the necessary academic training. But at the moment they are out in the street.
These are the things I am concerned with. I am concerned about the provision of schools. I am concerned about giving the boy who had to leave school before reaching the eighth or tenth grade a chance to go back for a year and pick up the knowledge of mathematics necessary to get into a trade course. If we do not meet these two requirements, then we shall be defeating the whole intention of the vocational training act.
I am not going to quarrel with any of the regulations or with what the minister had to say, but I do wish to emphasize these two points, because if they are not taken care of we will not be meeting the purpose of this legislation. I am not concerned whether we pass these vocational training regulations or not, because vocational training is designed to take care of the type of people with whom I am not concerned. The boy who gets through high school or obtains a university education is in a good position to wrestle for himself. But it is the thousands and thousands of victims of economic circumstances who do not get through school that vocational training should be designed to look after.
That is the angle I am concerned with, and I will wait until the bill comes before the house before I make any other observations on the matter.

The federal government should waste no time in getting together with the provincial governments and with the municipal authorities, in coming down to earth as men and saying, "Just how can this condition be remedied? These municipalities must bear in mind the fact that they have a terrific obligation towards those who will be the future taxpayers of Canada, namely the youth of their municipalities. Let not the municipalities slip out from under their burden. Let not the provincial governments fail to do their share. He is one of the most gallant gentlemen of this house.

At the end of the first war the government of the day took an interest in the matter of technical education, and special grants in aid were provided by the central government to the provincial governments to assist in the kind of work contemplated by the resolution introduced by the Minister of Labour today.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South, while he acknowledged the value of the kind of thing that is contemplated by the resolution, made a strong plea to provide for many other individuals who did not have the

The hon. member for Simcoe North also spoke of his disappointment that the Minister of Labour had not indicated at the beginning of his remarks his desire to co-operate with the provinces and with other bodies in the country in trying to make this effort really a great one. It is a good thing that from time to time in the House of Commons all parties should be able to forget their differences, as on the whole we are doing today, and direct our attention to a really important problem that has to do with a vital section of the younger generation of our country. But the Minister of Labour has given evidence of his conviction as to the desire and the necessity of co-operating with provincial governments in this matter.
Two years ago he convened, along with the Minister of Veterans Affairs and myself as Minister of National Health and Welfare, a conference that was held in Toronto with all of the provincial governments and with those groups in the nation interested in rehabilitation, vocational guidance and vocational training. That conference was one of the historic occasions of its kind in this country, and to the Minister of Labour, along with the provincial governments who were generous in their co-operation, must go the credit for the leadership that was given on that occasion and for the work that has been done since. Out of that meeting came a national advisory committee that is truly representative of the federal, provincial and voluntary bodies of this country interested in providing rehabilitation and vocational training for the people of our country. It is well that we should take this occasion to emphasize this work.
The relation to this resolution of the work of the Department of National Health and Welfare is this. The emphasis now on rehabilitation is one of the great steps and advances in medical science. No longer are we taking for granted that crippled people or people mentally ill or suffering from other

kinds of illnesses should regard themselves as incapable of playing their full part in the development of their own careers or of making the contribution that they would normally want to make to the nation.
I remember that not very long ago, shortly before I became Minister of National Health and Welfare, people who for instance were suffering from cerebral palsy were looked upon as unfortunate individuals who must no longer expect to live as normal human beings. That is not so in this country today. It is generally recognized that while the sufferer from cerebral palsy may not be able to become completely free of that terrible and unfortunate handicap, yet it is no longer necessary to regard the victim of that disease as incapable of playing any useful part in the life of the community.
I invite hon. members to go to the cerebral palsy centre in Ottawa. That centre is made possible out of grants provided by the service clubs and by the federal government under the national health program. There they will see the work of rehabilitation that is going on. It is one of the most satisfying experiences a man can have. I invite hon. members to go there and see the way in which some of the money provided by the taxpayers to the government is being expended for that particular group alone.
These people who are being given this training in the cerebral palsy centre, for instance, fall in with the kind of work that the Minister of Labour has in mind after they receive the basic training at the hands of a doctor and a nurse and are rendered more fit to look after themselves or to carry on their daily lives in a more normal way.
One could mention the work of the paraplegic association, in the aftermath of world war II. One of the most amazing achievements, surely, in our time is the work of the paraplegic association. I mention here the work of John Counsell, the head of that body, one of the great men of our country, a lad from Hamilton who lost the use of his limbs at Dieppe during the war, and who has taken a very active part in the paraplegic association. I am bold enough to say that some of the questions that are being asked might not have been asked if I had had a chance to speak first. I say that because I have been associated with the program of vocational training in the province of British Columbia, and in the whole of the Dominion of Canada, for the last 17 years, and have been actively associated with this particular program.
It was one of my hopes that I would be permitted to trace the origin of this program from its very early days down to the present day, because I think this program demonstrates the great opportunity which has been embraced by this government and the provincial governments to co-operate with one another. I think under this system of vocational training which we have now-not perfect, it is true-we have demonstrated the ability to work together and to co-operate province with province and provinces with the federal government better than under any other measure we have been able to suggest, except perhaps the program under the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The act which we are proposing to amend is one of the shorter acts on our statute books and I have no doubt that the amending bill will be short and contain only a few clauses. I rather suspect that because of its brevity it may be considered as of not too great importance. To my mind it is one of the most forward-looking pieces of legislation we shall have before us this session.
2632	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act
May I take a tew minutes to trace the origin of the vocational training program in Canada. Because of its modest beginnings and eventual importance it demonstrates the wisdom of starting with something very simple and being sure where you are going and building step by step to something worth while. It is a program that demands the partnership of the provinces as between themselves and the provinces with the federal government. The success of the many projects which have been operating under this program is, I think, testimony not only to the wisdom of those responsible for its early days but to the fact that ways can be found to solve any problem when the pressure of outside events brings together people of common aims and good will.
Because I am sure, more sure today than ever before, that some hon. members are only vaguely aware of the provisions of the vocational training act and what has been done under it, I propose, at the risk of being somewhat garrulous, to trace the growth of the operations under the present act from their early beginnings until the present day.
I hope in doing so to show that in the field of vocational training, as in many other fields, the policy of the government has been one of wise caution but firm decision once the right road ahead was clear.
Federal participation in education has always been a subject to be approached with great caution, but here we have a form of federal aid to education, as one hon. member has mentioned already. It is an example of the sensible approach. We find that it has resulted in the operation of many successful undertakings. Vocational training began during the depression years at the time when this government had funds allotted for what we called unemployment relief.
Much has been said about the hungry thirties, but it was during those days that methods were adopted to alleviate, in some small measure at any rate, the plight of young men and women who were without employment. Those of us who are old enough will remember that there were thousands of the youth of this country who had left school, who had no jobs, who had no opportunity for training, and who were just walking the streets. It was in those days, as part of the relief procedures, that the provinces and the dominion government-I am sorry if I inadvertently use the word "dominion" but we like it in British Columbia anyway; I may lapse into its use once in a while-at any rate the federal government made money available in co-operation with the provinces for some kind of training which would fit


the young people of those days for jobs which they hoped would eventuate sometime in the future.
Therefore classes were started, not only in the cities but in the rural areas, for young men and women between the ages of 16 and 25 years, I believe it was, which age limit was later extended to 30 years. Those young people received training in those classes and eventually found work. The employment services of Canada, together with many of the officials who were engaged on the program, co-operated in their placement. Because of their efforts we were able to alleviate to some degree the fear that we were training people for jobs that did not exist. That certainly was true for a time. Nevertheless as the program developed the worth of it became known, places were found and a great deal of good was done.
In those days we saw the beginnings of federal participation in physical health. We have an organization in British Columbia known as the PRO-REC, and it was in the days of the hungry thirties that the program of physical fitness had its beginning. I do not think I mentioned that, during those days, costs were shared on a 50-50 basis.
Because of the success-mind you, I am speaking now of 1938-of this program, this parliament decided to pass the Youth Training Act of 1939 under which the federal government authorized the continuation of those classes and the extension of the program. I am going to keep my remarks as short as I can, but I do want to say that under the Youth Training Act we were able to continue the program which had been established and to provide for other things as the need arose.
It is true that at that time war loomed its ugly head. Because we had these classes established in the provincial technical and vocational schools, as well as in rented quarters; because we had trained staffs of instructors it was possible with that foundation to build what eventually became known as the war emergency training program. We were able to carry on that program under the Youth Training Act with such amendments as were necessary under the War Measures Act. Mr. Chairman, I have sketched somewhat briefly the beginnings of what we are talking about today.
It is not my intention to bolster my story with statistics, as these can be found in the many reports of the Department of Labour dealing with vocational training, particularly in the Labour Gazette, which, as hon. members know, is published monthly. However, it may be interesting to know that from

April, 1940, to the end of 1944, upwards of 360,000 men and women were trained for the navy, army, air force and war industry at a total cost to the federal government of $21 million. The growth from those modest beginnings which I have attempted to show continued, and in 1942 the act we are now proposing to amend, the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, was passed.
May I go back just for a moment to say that because we had started in such a modest way and were gradually extending over a wide field, the federal authorities thought it wise to call together those in charge of the program to Ottawa at least twice a year for consultation. It was out of that kind of unofficial advisory body that authority was given to form the advisory council which now exists under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act.
In 1942, therefore, because of the changing nature of the work, it was thought wise to introduce the act known as the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act. It was thought desirable to co-ordinate the various activities then being carried on, to provide for the continuance of those which were desirable and to drop those no longer necessary.
I am sorry the hon. member for Cape Breton South is not at present in his seat, because I wanted to congratulate him for putting his finger, with his usual foresight, on the two great needs. Provincial departments of education, speaking on behalf of their governments, have always maintained that the federal government encouraged the provinces to build technical schools, as they did under the vocational education act of 1931, and after these schools had been built, with federal assistance, the provinces were left to carry on their operation. I believe we all know that vocational or technical schools, because of equipment requirements, usually have much smaller classes but higher paid staffs. At any rate, they are more expensive schools to operate, yet no money was allocated from federal funds to assist in the operation of these schools once they were built.
However, that was remedied by the passing of the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, because under that act provision was made, not only for funds for capital expenditure, but also funds on an annual basis to assist in the operation of these schools. Perhaps the hon. member for Cape Breton South is not aware of that provision under the present act. The vocational training act provides for both these needs, modestly it is true, but the door is ajar; and there are those

Vocational Training Co-ordination Act of us still around who are ready to give it a vigorous shove in order to push it wide open, if we get the chance.
By the end of the war there were a number of separate agreements between the federal authorities and the various provinces, and these covered a variety of activities by various definite schedules, providing for every class and age group of citizens. The vocational schools assistance agreement, to which the minister already referred, provided for capital and operational grants for a period, I believe, of ten years, The youth training agreement, already mentioned, was for unemployed youths who had never been employed and who were in that age group which needed some form of training in order to assist them to secure employment. Under the urban and rural occupational training, provision was made for those who had been employed, were out of a job, and who required training, or retraining, to fit them for a different type of job. Then we had training for war industries and for the armed services and the great rehabilitation program for veterans of the second world war, all of which were carried out under the same authority in co-operation with and at the request of the Department of Veterans Affairs. There was another great program, Mr. Chairman, on which I could talk for hours. We called it preuniversity training for veterans of the second world war. An hon. member opposite mentioned the fact that sometimes the veteran who had come back had less academic training than he could have had because, due to the war, he was prevented from going on with further education. That was certainly true with many of the veterans who, had there not been a war, probably would have gone to university.
The officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs, for whom I have the greatest admiration because of what they did for the veterans of the last war, recognized that situation. They recognized that there were many men and women who had enlisted in the services who would have gone to university but who unfortunately were not properly prepared for it. Because of that fact, schools were established all over the country for the purpose of providing pre-university training; and I am sure you would be amazed, Mr. Chairman, to learn the number of people we were able to bring up to university entrance standards, young men and women with no previous education beyond grade 10. Further than that, they did better work in the university than students from the regular schools. That was probably because we

I have often heard the question asked in this house and outside as to why we do not provide for students who should go to university but who cannot afford to do so. We do provide that opportunity, and have been doing so since 1939.
Before I develop that, permit me to recite all these activities to show how comprehensive the program has become. When brought together these programs provide this pattern. There was federal aid for education at the secondary school level and capital expenditure for the operation of schools run by provincial authorities. There were classes for youngsters who had left school but who had no previous training at all. There were classes for those who had been employed but were out of work and wanted to change their jobs. There were classes for veterans and for older people, and correspondence classes for those in remote areas. The council, which has already been referred to, considered all these things and made recommendations. We therefore had a comprehensive program brought together under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, paid for in most cases on a 50-50 basis with the provinces, except for those portions which dealt with war services or training for members of the armed forces.
May I say for the benefit of the hon. member for Simcoe North that we did have classes for young veterans who lacked academic training, which provided training similar to the type we gave at the end of the war to veterans who wished to go to university and which I described previously as preuniversity training. There are classes operating today for young soldiers who lack the required academic standards.
Federal expenditures covering all these programs since their inception in 1939-and I took the trouble to check this figure- amount at the present time to a little short of $90 million.
Reverting to the student aid program which is carried on in co-operation with the provinces. I might point out that this has been in operation since 1939. If I quote figures from my own province of British Columbia it is only because I happen to know them better than the figures relating to other provinces, though I do know that these other provinces have similar programs. From a very modest beginning in 1939, when the province and the federal authorities each contributed $2,550 or a total of $5,100, the


scheme has grown until today, and for some years past, each government has made available $30,000 per year. To that amount the local government in British Columbia adds another $50,000 for loans, so that we have a total of a little more than $110,000 available every year to assist needy students of intellectual capacity to go to university.
It is interesting, Mr. Chairman, and very heartening to learn that in the province of British Columbia alone, regardless of the others, 5,765 young men and women have been assisted in obtaining further education. At the present moment there are 627 young British Columbians attending university because of assistance provided under this fund. I do not know the figures for the present year for the whole country but for last year, the academic year 1952-53, there were 4,663 students attending the universities of Canada under this fund, and of those some 1,098 were women.
All the activities which I have described were sponsored and directed by the training branch of the Department of Labour, and have been recommended to the ministry by an advisory council. I know it is understood that, because of changing conditions, modifications in the composition of the council itself are required. I should like to discuss that matter for a moment. This advisory council grew out of a need. In the early days we had this unofficial council-it was not really unofficial, but it was gathered together without any statutory provision-to discuss these matters. We met with the director of training. I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that I keep slipping in a "we" once in a while, but I happened to be one of them. It was necessary then for us to meet to advise the minister on those matters which we thought wise, to recommend that the scheme be enlarged, and to assess the need for additional programs.
I do not know whether it is permissible in this chamber to pay tribute to an official by name, but 1 should like to place on record the admiration of all who knew him for the late Mr. R. F. Thompson, who was director of training in the Department of Labour. It was he who sparked the program and directed it from its early days until he died, quite recently. It was because of his industry and his ability to secure the cooperation of all manner of people throughout this country that we have such a measure on the statute books today.
On this council I have mentioned it was originally intended to have representatives in equal number of labour and industry. We have had representatives of labour, industry, womens' organizations, agriculture, veterans

organizations and education. Not all provinces were officially represented. As a matter of fact, there were only three representatives of education.
I do not know the details of the amending bill, but the resolution we are discussing leads me to suppose that the purpose of increasing the number of the council is so that a representative of all ten provinces may find a place on it. The present bill provides for a chairman and 16 members. I know the resolution calls for an increase in the number, and I think that is why. Where the provinces are co-operating, as they are, willingly and anxiously, I think it is only right that they should have an official place on the council, and I believe that is what the minister has in mind.
There is one last subject that I wish to mention. I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke very feelingly, as he always does, about this question of rehabilitation of the physically handicapped. It is one of the newer programs that have been operating under this act. It has to do with the training or retraining of those suffering physical handicaps. Much was learned over all these years from what has been done by the Department of Veterans Affairs, from the programs carried out in several of the provinces under the various workmen's compensation acts, and from the program we had ourselves, because we trained handicapped persons too. Those successful experiences have encouraged everybody connected with this program to the point of enthusiasm, I might say, as to the possibility of doing a great and noble work.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has announced a measure for the relief of those totally disabled. I am hopeful that this amending bill will contain provision for adequate funds and means for an all-out attack on a problem which must touch the emotions of all hon. members as well as commend itself to us all as a sound economic measure.
When I spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I mentioned this subject and pointed out that men and women suffering a physical handicap can and should be trained for occupations they are capable of performing. There is a tremendous waste of talent when we allow such persons to swell the ranks of the unemployed. The last thing they want is sympathy, although that we must give in full measure. The best kind of sympathy is the opportunity to become selfsupporting and self-respecting. This can be done. It has been done and it is now being done. What is needed now is authority to make it a major undertaking.
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act
I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members realize that it is not only the right thing but the wise thing to do. This act will make it possible to engage the resourcefulness of those now interested in the medical and physical rehabilitation of those who suffer a handicap from whatever cause. Mention was made of voluntary agencies.
I think it was the hon. member for Hamilton West who asked whether the training would be done in schools or in industry or through the various agencies. The minister mentioned the paraplegic association, the cerebral palsy association, and so on. It is the intention- in fact it is being done now-to co-ordinate the efforts of those agencies and give the training wherever it can best be done.
I conclude by saying that throughout this country there are numerous organizations actively concerned with this problem I have just mentioned. They are all anxious to get going once we have a co-ordinator. They want the activities in these matters brought together. They want somebody to head it; they are going to get it under this act. They are seized with enthusiasm about what can be done. They await only some central authority to co-ordinate their services in a common effort. The provinces are willing. This measure, which authorizes the federal government and particularly the Department of Labour to be that co-ordinating agency, is one which, I suggest, will commend itself to all hon. members.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as my colleagues the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Saskatoon have already pointed out, we welcome the introduction of this resolution. I imagine it would be fair to say that ministers generally, when they introduce matters which they must pilot through the house, like to get them through as rapidly as possible; but this afternoon I believe the Minister of Labour is really quite pleased that a fair amount of time is being spent on this important piece of legislation.
We all listened with considerable interest to the highly informative speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) who in his former capacity as deputy minister of education in one of our provinces had considerable to do with technical education. In passing may I say that we in the province of Manitoba appreciate the assistance that has come our way under this program. We are particularly pleased with and proud of our technical vocational school in the city of Winnipeg.
2636	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act
As my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon has pointed out, we are interested in all possible education for the young people of this country, and we are indeed pleased to see this form of federal assistance to education. No one suggests that it interferes in any way with the complete jurisdiction over education which is accorded to the provinces by section 92 of the British North America Act. Rather the financial assistance provided in this way is for the benefit of the country as a whole. We hope to see that principle extended to still other areas of education.
However, Mr. Chairman, since my colleagues and the members of other parties have spoken on those aspects of the matter I shall not take further time on them. Rather I wanted to say a few words concerning the aspect of this legislation which was touched upon by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who referred to the fact that the resolution states that the measure to be introduced will include authority to enter into agreements with the provinces to grant assistance for the rehabilitation training of disabled persons.
I am sure we all share the sentiments expressed by the minister this afternoon when he pointed out that society has progressed to the point, and medical science has served us to the point, where disabled people no longer have to be regarded as useless to society or to themselves. There still are people who suffer very great misfortunes and disabilities, but the number of people who can lead happy and useful lives, despite physical disabilities of one kind and another, is steadily increasing due in part to the progress of medical science and in part to the attitude of society in accepting the responsibility to provide funds to help such people.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the main point I want to make in connection with this is my very strong feeling that there must be the closest co-operation between the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Health and Welfare in connection with the rehabilitation program and pensions to disabled persons. I know the immediate answer of those two ministers will be that they co-operate all the time. What I am asking for now is something more than just co-operation in the sense that they get together personally. I feel that these two pieces of legislation, the one before us now in the name of the Minister of Labour and the one the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be bringing in shortly, must be dovetailed together. From what we have before us now and from the sketchy information we have about the other legislation, my fear is that our disabled people are going to be put into one category or the other. There 

are going to be those for whom rehabilitation training will be useful and they will get that, whereas others will be regarded as totally disabled and they will get the disability pension provided they meet the means test.
As I say, the information we have had with respect to the legislation that is yet to come is sketchy, but it has been suggested that the pensions to be provided under that legislation will be only for those who are totally and permanently disabled. I do not think it should be that way. I feel the very fact that the Minister of Labour is now introducing a provision for a rehabilitation program calls for dealing with these two matters together. In my view there are people who are capable of taking a certain amount of rehabilitation training which means that they are not permanently disabled; but in order to take that training and get a start, they will need some financial assistance. On the other hand the fact that the'y are not permanently disabled may bar them from getting the pension. I hope that the hard and fast line which I see looming up will not be drawn, but that there will be a common sense and a humanitarian approach to this whole problem.
It is a great venture upon which we are launching, in that we are proposing to spend public money to try and do something worthwhile for disabled persons. This is a good move. Let us not scuttle the program by this hard and fast line I fear may be drawn. Let us admit that there will be some people for whom the only thing we can do is provide pensions. If that is the case, let us do that and let us make these pensions decent and adequate. There will be other persons who do not need pensions at the moment, but who do need rehabilitation training. Let us see that they get the kind of rehabilitation training that will be useful to them. Let us not forget that there will be a third group who are neither wholly in one category nor wholly in the other. I hope these people will not be shifted from one category to the other, and end up getting nothing at all. They need rehabilitation training, and financial assistance while they are taking that training.
As I say, I plead not only for close cooperation between the two ministers concerned, but co-operation between them and the Minister of Veterans Affairs as well. I plead for the legislation to be dovetailed together in such a way that it will provide the utmost benefit to our disabled persons, who need and deserve everything we can do for them.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
When one agrees with a measure it seems hardly necessary for him to indulge in extended debate in order to indicate his

position. All those sitting with me agree wholeheartedly with the purpose of this resolution. We have spoken before when measures designed to amend the act have been before us.
It is noted in the resolution that it is deemed advisable to amend the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act to meet the requirements, first of defence, and second, other purposes. We feel, of course, that at a time like this, when defence is so essential, it is most important that we extend the act in such a way as to fully utilize the services of the largest possible number of Canadians.
However, if there were no need for defence we would still say that an act of this kind would be wholly necessary, and that every effort should be made by the federal government, working in co-operation with the provincial governments, to expand the program in its application to disabled persons. I agree that a step forward was taken when it was proposed that pensions would be paid to certain of our disabled people. I also agree fully with those who have asserted that there is something just as important, probably even more important, and that is providing training for those who are capable of being trained even though they are disabled. I have talked with a number of these people. They ask not for charity, although they realize there are certain of their numbers who are totally disabled or cannot be trained. At the same time they have stressed the fact that the disabled who can take advantage of the training want the training.
We certainly support the measure, particularly as it relates to the training of disabled persons. There were a number of things which I intended to say concerning the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, but I have thought it over and I believe it would be more appropriate for me to say those things when we are dealing with the estimates relating to vocational training. I simply say to the minister that we support the resolution. We feel that it will perform a most useful function for our Canadian people and for Canada.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the need for broader facilities for vocational training in Canada is one of the great educational needs of our time. We have been passing through a technological revolution which has resulted in a great demand for trained technicians to man the machines of our mechanized civilization. Notwithstanding that fact, our high schools still continue to stress the straight academic program and
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act preparation for the professions rather than preparation for the technical pursuits that are so necessary today.
As I have listened to the discussion thus far I have come to the conclusion that the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act recognizes this need. I am glad I did not speak before the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, because I feel he has made an excellent and most enlightening contribution to the debate. I was keenly interested in the survey he made of the history of this particular legislation.
Notwithstanding the fact that there have been measures promoting vocational training in Canada now for a considerable number of years, and that this act has been in effect since 1942, as I have already intimated there is still a great need for the expansion of vocational training facilities. I believe the major drawback in meeting this need for vocational training arises from the bugbear of all education today, the financial problem.
As I look at the act it seems to me that the carrying out of its various measures must depend upon provincial initiative. Unfortunately, as all hon. members are aware, our provinces are already burdened with education costs. Therefore they are reluctant to take any action that would increase in any way their financial obligations in the matter of education. So in the final analysis the responsibility for action falls back upon the municipalities.
During the resolution stage of the discussion, for my own information, I would like to ask the minister one or two questions concerning which he might be able to enlighten me. Would there be financial assistance for agricultural schools which operate mainly for rural young people who have not had the advantage of formal high school education? I give as an example an agricultural school that provides training in the basic skills required for farming, a general practical course in farming operations for farm boys, and for the farm girls a basic training in home economics or the skills required for home-making. It seems to me that schedule "O" might provide for financial assistance to a program of this kind, and I was wondering if that interpretation would be correct.
Another query that comes to mind is this. Is financial assistance under this act possible for a large school area program, which endeavours to meet the demand for a broadened curriculum, and also the necessity for providing adequate facilities to meet the new
2638	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act demands in educational circles today? The large school area program has not been too successful to date in my own province. As a matter of fact we have established only one area, chiefly because the various communities are suspicious that a broadening of educational facilities in this way would entail large increases in the costs of education. I would hope that a program of this kind, where there is an attempt to introduce training in technical skills, in farm skills and in commercial lines, as well as giving the regular basic collegiate program, should come in for assistance under this act. Certainly it might encourage a more rapid acceptance of this new idea in educational circles.
I wonder, too, if there is any provision in the act for vocational guidance. When we begin to specialize in the field of education the problem immediately arises as to the necessity for offering special counsel and advice to our young people in the matter of selecting their areas of interest. The vocational guidance movement has emerged in Canada since 1930 to meet this need. I have looked through recent reports concerning the administration of the act, and I cannot see any specific reference to provision being made for financial assistance in the carrying on of a vocational guidance program. Perhaps the minister could give us some information on that point.
I see a possible solution in the very title of the act for some of the difficulties I have outlined. The act is known as the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, and the word "co-ordination" suggests to me one method of broadening the scope of this particular legislation. I note in the schedule of payments that for vocational training programs covering members of the armed forces and war veterans the federal government provides support to the extent of 100 per cent, whereas in the training of disabled persons and young people between the ages of 16 and 30, with particular reference in schedule "O" to the training of foremen, supervisors and the like, the support is either 75 per cent or 50 per cent.
We know that in military matters considerations of cost are never involved. It seems to me some attempt might be made to bring about a closer integration of the technical training required to meet the demands of a technological civilization as well as the technical training required to meet the demands of our defence program. While these activities parallel one another to some


extent, they do tend to have separate treatment. Independent facilities are established which obviously would increase considerably the expenditures involved.
In the world of today the areas of civilian and military activities seem to be almost indivisible, because in a time of trouble, in a time of war, everyone would be caught up in the demands of defence. It should be in our best interests to explore every possible avenue whereby we might meet the growing demand for a larger number of people with training in the technical skills. Preparedness is the best defence in the long run, and I hope this suggestion might be given attention as amendments to the act are brought in when we finally have the bill before us.
One final word, Mr. Chairman. There would appear to be a need for some publicity on behalf of the activities under this act. I note that in the report for 1952 there are regional directors in every province, with the exception of British Columbia, Manitoba and Newfoundland. The maritime provinces are particularly well represented from the standpoint of regional directors. I would imagine that a regional director is largely responsible for applying the terms of the act to the situation as he finds it in his particular province. It might be that if we had a wider representation-for example, if there were regional directors in the other provinces which do not have such persons at the present time-these people would provide the necessary leadership in taking advantage of all the measures under the act and applying them to the situation they find in their particular provinces. There are provisions in the act, I am sure, that even those in educational circles are not aware of, provisions that would assist in a real way in meeting the demands for vocational training.
May I close by saying a few words with regard to the section dealing with bursaries for student aid. I note that this provision was established in 1939. It makes possible payment of up to $400, I believe, in the case of deserving students desiring to go on to some phase of university training. I wonder whether any consideration has been given to the changed cost situation obtaining today as compared with that existing in 1939. A bursary of $400 does not go very far today in meeting the cost of a university education. In fact in some universities it would hardly cover the tuition fees. That thought occurred to me as I read through the latest report on the administration of this act.
Again, I feel that there is a need for wider publicity concerning opportunities provided under this schedule. If we had a full-time

regional director, a regional representative in the province of Manitoba, many more students might be encouraged to take advantage of the provisions of this legislation.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to make just a few remarks on this resolution. I should like to read the part in which I am interested:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act to meet present-day requirements for defence and other purposes.
I like the way it is worded, "to meet present-day requirements for defence and other purposes". Everyone knows that years ago skilled mechanics spent long years of their lives, at very little pay, learning their trade. Present-day requirements are much different. First, we are short of labour, or we have been for the past number of years. Ever since 1939 we have been short of labour, and it has been necessary to use these men who have learned their skills in productive work in a manner that was not conceived years ago when we had the apprenticeship system in operation. Today we have learned that students, by adapting themselves properly in the proper environment, can become productive much more rapidly than they could under the old apprenticeship system. Thus I am glad to see the government and our own Minister of Labour introducing a resolution to amend the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act to meet present-day requirements for defence and other purposes.
The most important responsibility of any government is to provide the opportunity for the citizens of that country to have employment. Everyone has seen in the past number of years that as long as there is full employment there are good times. That is the main requirement for the success and progress of a country. Each person in the country who has been trained in one of our vocational training schools generally provides jobs for three or four helpers who may not be as skilled as he is.
I would refer to the splendid work that our vocational schools have done in turning out electricians, carpenters, automobile mechanics, diesel engine mechanics and many others in the past. Today the need for vocational training is changing. When we look around this room, for instance, and notice the number of microphones and loudspeakers that are present, we can see that it requires men with the proper vocational training to maintain this equipment. Everyone knows that unless there are the proper courses available it is very difficult for men to learn the job of maintaining this equipment.
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act
We have television, and we have the new jet engines. The developments in atomic energy have been tremendous. In all these fields the requirements for skilled mechanics to produce, maintain and keep in operation all these new pieces of apparatus are staggering. Today it is the responsibility of this government to go into fields which, under the British North America Act, could well be considered none of their business, so that we may have at the disposal of this nation men with the technical knowledge required to keep us in fair competition, both in business and in defence, with other nations.
We have heard many times that the Russians have outstripped us in their education of scientific men. If we had not seen during the Korean conflict how they have devised machines which have bettered our own equipment, which we thought was the best in the world, we might not have been inclined to go along with that belief. But after having had a demonstration of their equipment it is easy to believe that perhaps they have outstripped us in the production of scientists and engineers.
If that is true the academic side of our educational system must be improved. Although education is the responsibility of the municipality and therefore comes under the jurisdiction of the province, when it becomes a national issue as to whether we have enough scientists and engineers, then it becomes the problem of the dominion government. At the last session we passed legislation to help increase the number of scientists and engineers to produce the equipment necessary to be competitive in an industrial way and also for defence purposes. Now we must have the vocationally trained men, men with trades ability, to maintain the equipment put into the hands of the people of our country by the scientists and engineers.
Thus it is my contention that we should give favourable consideration to this resolution to amend the Vocational Training Coordination Act in order to meet present-day requirements for defence and other purposes. I should like to hear the minister, some time before this bill is completed, state just what proportion the dominion government is prepared to pay in connection with the financing of the construction of vocational schools. The need in some localities is considerable.
I know the vocational school in my riding is out of date. It is equipped to perform the services I mentioned at the beginning of my speech. It does a good job of training carpenters, bricklayers, machinists and mechanics, but it is not in position to turn out
2640	HOUSE OF
Vocational Training Co-ordination Act men competent to deal with the new electronic problems that lace this nation today. This is one of the growing needs in many parts of the country, and certainly in my own riding we need a new vocational school adequate and up to date to handle the problems that face the young Canadians in that area.
I am told that this Liberal government is prepared to match donations with the provincial governments on projects of this kind, but I should like to have the Minister of Labour state that this is the dominion government's policy with regard to assisting municipalities in their efforts to build these schools. The demand for trained men to protect the country, to fulfil the requirements of the armed services, and to make this country competitive with other countries in the markets of the world, is such that it becomes a dominion responsibility to assist those people who pay taxes locally. I should like to hear just what the dominion government proposes to do.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks in connection with this resolution. The Minister of National Health and Welfare referred to the rehabilitation centre outside Ottawa. This centre has done a great work. I know something of what it has done since its inauguration many years ago. That centre was established by the lumbermen's safety association of the province of Ontario for the rehabilitation of maimed and disabled lumberjacks, and it did great work in that respect. Then the war came along and the dominion government- I make no apology for using the word "dominion"-needed something of this sort. It was taken over and made larger, bigger and better in every way. It has done great work over the years in rehabilitation, but I think they could have gone further in connection with vocational training. They have not done very much along that line, and there is room for improvement. I hope that there will be a change in that connection.
The resolution reads in part:
-for defence and other purposes, including authority to enter into agreements with the provinces to grant assistance for rehabilitation training of disabled persons-
I do not think the resolution goes far enough, although I am glad the dominion government is ready to go along with the provinces in connection with recreational and vocational training. Today the province of Ontario will make a grant of $5,000 toward the erection of a building for recreational and vocational training, and I do not know why the dominion government should not make a similar grant. I should like to hear


from the minister in that respect. They should at least give dollar for dollar with the provinces in this respect.
We have a new school in our town, but it finds itself cramped in the carrying on of recreational and vocational training. We tried to carry on this program even before we had the new school but found it financially impossible to continue to employ a recreational director. We had to dispense with him a year or two ago. If the department would come along and make a grant in aid for recreational and vocational training that program could be continued in that little town, I am sure it would be appreciated, and I think the government should go that far. This bill does not say how far the government will go, but probably the minister will tell us when he comes to answer.
A great need in the country today is for nurses. If a bomb were dropped today in Ottawa or in any part of Canada the first people needed would be nurses. They are the first people needed to help the maimed, the sick and the dying. They have been a great asset to Canada in the past and I know they will be in the future. Many young women who would become good nurses find it financially impossible to undertake the training. I think the department could go a little further with this bill and agree to pay $10 a week to every girl in Canada who would take up nursing training.
Some hon. member referred to the need of additional training for nurses. Certain nurses might require some extra training. Those nurses who go into the far north on government projects or to Red Cross outposts probably should have some extra training along medical lines, because in many cases they are a great many miles from a doctor. I think the department should go so far as to say that any young girl who was willing to sign up for three or five years to go to distant places like this would have her extra training paid for the one year or whatever time it might take to qualify such a girl for the position. We are short of nurses in Canada today even without an emergency. We could use at least 25 per cent more nurses in Canada. Something must be done to encourage young girls to take up this work.
Then I spoke of rehabilitation grants to schools. This would prove a great asset to our country and to our young people. Someone said that our jails and institutions are completely full. I do not believe our country is as bad as that. I believe that we are probably better than average compared with other countries in that respect. However, we are not good enough. Our young people should

be better; and if they were given the opportunity of obtaining training such as this legislation starts out to provide, and if it would go a little further than is mentioned in this resolution, then I believe we would not only all have a better place in which to live, but the young people of Canada could be improved and at the same time assist in the future development of Canada.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to add just one word. I have listened with respect to everything said in the house this afternoon. I am delighted to hear of the good work being done, and I approve wholeheartedly of projects for the extension of such work. However, none of us in this house believe that life consists wholly in things which come from vocational training, I mean things which are made by the teaching of various skills. We know that life does not consist wholly of these things, and I hope with these young people it will be possible in the course of the development of these skills also to introduce them to some of the thoughts of the great and good people who have made our civilization what it is.
It seems to me it would be a thousand pities if in the course of acquiring skills no attempt was made or time provided to turn their minds to these other things. I have just one practical suggestion to make and it is this. I believe there is no subject comparable to biography in developing in one's mind an appreciation of these things, and it seems to me there could be no better way of accomplishing that than by providing for that study perhaps in the sphere in which these young people are being trained, so their minds may be turned toward benefiting from the thoughts of people who have excelled in that particular sphere and who also had a broad view of life and realized that it did not consist wholly of the things that we touch, taste and handle.

subsubtopic: VOCATIONAL TRAINING CO-ORDINATION ACT AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:

The hon. member for Hamilton West asked if I would state how disabled persons will be trained. I believe that was the general nature of the question. Let me state at once the reason the rehabilitation of disabled persons appears in this bill. As hon. members know, during the past few years we have been training disabled persons under existing schedules in the federal-provincial training agreements. The reason special authority is being asked in this legislation is so that we will be able to make, in conjunction with the provinces, special arrangements with regard to the disabled.
My colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare this afternoon gave a hint of the rehabilitation program which is now being carried out in conjunction with the provinces. He referred to that portion of it devoted to medical rehabilitation which he will be bringing forward again this year. As he pointed out, as soon as the medical teams have done what they can to repair disabled persons and the doctors and psychologists have completed their technical work and provided all assistance that can be given under the medical banner, then the vocational training people will be standing by ready to take the disabled person over with a full knowledge of what has happened medically. They will then, where needed, get vocational training under provincial jurisdiction, with part of the cost being borne by the federal government.
Right there I think I could give the answer to a part of the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Both at the medical phase of rehabilitation and then when we come into the second of the three phases-they are the medical, the training and the placement-we realize that there will be a need for special treatment of these disabled people, something which was not necessary for fit people who came in under well classified schedules. Hence we are visualizing the possibility, in conjunction with the provinces, where needed, of taking care of individual financial needs to make it possible for the disabled person to go and


get the training. If that disabled person has special financial responsibilities while the training is being given, the program is so planned as to make it possible to help take care of that matter until the person has been able to gain the skill that can help to make him self-supporting, then the placement officials of the national employment service- who will then be even more highly skilled, I hope, than they are now-will take him over and so fit him into a job in industry on the basis of his value to industry and not in any sense on the basis of pity. These people, when they are trained-if they are properly trained-and their capacities are sharpened up, will be able to serve in industry just as well and just as valuably as do the able-bodied people at their sides.
