subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing this resolution I should like to state that the proposal to amend the Pension Act at this time does not arise from any changes in the basic rates of pensions paid to disabled veterans, nor does it depart from any of the major principles underlying this legislation. Rather it is intended to confer some additional benefits upon certain dependents of veterans and to remove certain difficulties which have arisen in the administration of the act and in its interpretation by the commission.
I believe all hon. members will agree with me that, in general, the provisions of the Canadian Pension Act have been warmly approved and generously interpreted. And that is as it should be. I believe it is the general desire of the Canadian public that those who have suffered from service to their country, and the dependents of these people, should be adequately compensated.
Without going into any details of the bill which will follow the resolution, perhaps I might explain some of the major amendments. One which I am sure will meet with the approval of all members of the committee is a provision to allow the commission to pay pensions for adopted children of pensioners. For a number of years now members on both sides of the house have joined with the various national veteran bodies in the country in urging that consideration be given to such a measure. This proposal has had my own sympathetic support, and I must say I was very pleased to recommend to the government that in this bill an amendment should be introduced to empower the commission to pay pensions in respect of children legally adopted by a pensioner, subsequent to the appearance of an injury or disease for which he is pensioned.
I believe the restriction that has existed heretofore was in the act to protect the child as well as the treasury against a practice known as baby farming, which might have existed some years back. It is felt now that adoption legislation in the various provinces provides sufficient protection, and that the commission is capable of protecting both the child and the treasury of the state in this connection. Therefore I am happy to introduce that amendment to the Pension Act. Of course the amendment will also maintain

Pension Act
the right to pension of legitimate children born to the pensioner subsequent to the injury or disease for which he is pensioned.
Another major amendment to the act will advance the cut-off date for the marriage of pensioned veterans of world war I. The house will recall that in 1951 the cut-off date was advanced from 1948 to May 1, 1951. This was the most recent of several changes made in the act concerning this dateline, and it is now proposed to recognize wives of pensioners who were married prior to January 1, 1954.
On this particular point I have been asked this question. Why not abolish the dateline altogether, since it is now 36 years since the end of world war I. I confess that at first glance I felt this suggestion had merit. However, on further consideration I have recommended an advance in the dateline which, I believe, was first introduced in May, 1933. I believe the reason for fixing a dateline was to protect the veteran and the treasury from so-called deathbed marriages between aged pensioners and very much younger wives who it was felt might have some mercenary motives. I must say that I have never thought this was very flattering to womanhood in general.
However, with the average age of world war I veterans steadily climbing, it seemed wiser to retain the dateline to protect the sound marriages and retain the terms which this method provides, because under the act as it exists today the wife of a pensioner who is in receipt of a pension of 50 per cent or over-that is, from 50 per cent to 100 per cent-automatically becomes the recipient of a widow's pension of $100 a month when the veteran dies, provided that she is otherwise qualified; that is, that the marriage was a legal one and the widow has not disentitled herself. I believe this generous provision merits the protection that a cut-off date for marriages provides.
Another feature of the bill concerns helplessness allowances. As hon. members know, helplessness allowance is paid to very seriously disabled veterans who need to have constant attention. This allowance is paid to them over and above the pension. The allowance can be from $480 up to $1,400. However, when the pensioner is in one of the departmental institutions for treatment and attendance is provided for him, the helplessness allowance is stopped. It has been

found that many of these cases, after having been in the hospital for some time and having returned home, remain as what are called outpatients of the hospital. They are still on the departmental strength as outpatients, and the act as it exists has created some difficulty in permitting the commission to give such a pensioner the helplessness allowance which he was receiving before entering hospital. Fortunately there are not too many of these seriously disabled pensioners who must have helplessness allowances. I believe there are slightly over 1,000, distributed between world war I and world war II veterans. Others of course need to have constant attendance, but they are looked after in our institutions.
The other amendments, Mr. Chairman, are designed to facilitate the administration of the act by conforming with terms used by the department and by the commission, and they clarify certain powers vested in appeal boards of the commission.
Finally, as the resolution specifies, it is intended to introduce an amendment to permit the salaries of the members of the pension commission to be determined by the governor in council rather than by statute as it exists at the present time. This is really for the purpose of permitting, when it is felt that increases are justified, the commissioners to be adequately compensated, without it being necessary to introduce a bill. It is the pattern which is followed, I understand, in most governmental bodies set up as this commission is. Of course parliament has control of this money, as an item must be provided in the estimates to pay those salaries.
As I stated, Mr. Chairman, the changes in this amending bill do not involve any major new expenditures. They are designed more to make the administration of the act uniform and equitable and to tailor the procedures to present-day needs.
